projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charles Douglas Pritchett was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: This is July the 19th, 2004. We're in Cataula, Georgia, doing an interview of Charles Douglas Pritchett. His birthdate is [redacted]. He served in the U.S. Navy Amphibious Forces during World War II.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Mr. Pritchett, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Drafted.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Can you tell me where you were living at the time?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Here in Cataula.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Can you tell me why you picked the branch of service that you chose?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Well, you didn't pick. At that time you were just placed. So I had no choice. However, I did have a choice from the standpoint once I got in the Navy as to where I, to some extent, the Amphibious Forces because I received extra compensation for serving in that. And I had a family back at home that needed all the compensation we could get, so I volunteered for the Amphibious Forces.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in service?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Frightened to no end. No, not particularly, other than the fact, I suppose, that prior to that time about the only names that I was ever familiar with were Johnsons and Browns and Smiths and Joneses, and when I got into the muster, as we call it, the roll call, and they started using such names as Kolakowski (phonetic), Evashevski (phonetic), things of that nature, I thought I must have been in some foreign service instead of service to the United States.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Can you tell us about your boot camp training?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Well, it was rush, rush, rush. Sometimes wait, wait, wait. Primarily just continuous subjected to all kinds of activities that I was totally unfamiliar with. I went into the service off the farm and thought I was somewhat in good physical condition, but I never done any calisthenics, I never done any pushups and things of that nature. So rather early I learned that I was, as a Georgia farm boy, I wasn't in nearly good condition that the military expected of me. So it was rather strenuous exercises.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No. No, ma'am, I don't.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Okay. How did you get through it, through your basic training?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: One day at a time. One hour at a time.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: And you served in World War II. Is that correct?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I was first sent to Atlanta. From there on a matter of a few hours I was sent to Bainbridge, naval operating station in Bainbridge, Maryland. And from there, after basic training which was, I believe around six weeks, I was sent in to the Amphibious Forces training at Little Creek, Virginia, which is on the coast there in, near Norfolk, Virginia. And from there a couple weeks in advanced amphibious service at Solomons, Maryland. And that was the basic, that was the extent of my basic training and then I was sent overseas.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: What was your active duty, sir? Where did you go while you were sent overseas? Where did you go there?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: First we went to North Africa. The first place I went was a place called Brasilia, which was in Tunisia. And from there we went to Oran, Algiers, and Algeria, which is the capital of -- Algiers, which is the capital of Algeria. We get into Italy, Corsica, Island of Elba, and France.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: And what was your job assignment?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I was a boatswain's mate or coxswain, as they called them, which was operating an LCVP, which is a landing craft, vehicle, personnel, which is a small naval unit which transports the soldiers and Marines from the larger ships to the beaches during invasions.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Did you see combat?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Yes, ma'am. In three different battles: Anzio, Island of Elba, and France.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Were there many casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Not so many in my unit, but when I refer to a unit, I refer to the small vessel that I operated on. But on our larger vessel, which I was -- we called it our mother ship, my boat hung at what they called a davit on board an LST, which is a landing ship tank which has a -- 628 feet long -- has a crew of about 200 men which we were just attached to that. My little unit was only five men: myself and four other amphibious men. We only had two casualties -- injuries, but no fatalities, but we had a number of fatalities during the different battles off of my ship and all the other ships that were operating with us. The invasions -- invasions was a very frustrating time. We generally anchored off the coast some eight to ten miles. My little boat was then let down into the water. My crew and myself handled the boat, me being the boatswain's mate, it was my response- -- the boat was basically my responsibility. I had a signal man, a gunner, a radio operator, and a mechanic in my unit. And we took on 36 men, 36 troops and then we followed the instructions as to what we were -- how we were to proceed and then we proceeded into the beaches and landed. And at that time, of course, you're probably familiar with some various movies in which you may have seen what takes place during the invasions.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: What invasions were you involved in?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Anzio and the Island of Elba and France.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: And in France, what --

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Well, this was in southern France on August 15th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: What was the highest rank you achieved?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Boatswain's Mate First Class, which in the Army is equivalent to Sergeant First Class.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family during this time?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Through letter writing. There were no telephones available.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: What was the food like while you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Acceptable (laughter).

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Well, what there was, yes. We always desired other things, naturally, just as we do, I suppose, today in civilian life, but they were sufficient to keep us in physical -- be physically fit.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Did you feel any stress or pressure during this time?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Well, as an 18-, 19-, 20-, 21-year-old, there was a tremendous amount of desire to be at home. There was a tremendous amount of questions floating in our minds wondering if people back home really knew what we were enduring, and basically from time to time we questioned whether or not what we were doing was beneficial. I mean, we were -- me, from Harris County, I was dumb as a doorknob, anyways, from the standpoint of history, and it was somewhat of a time of confusion more than distress.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Was there anything that you did special for good luck?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Never thought about that, no. No, I didn't have any suspicions. Always hoping that, you know, you would see the tomorrow and that those around you would likewise see tomorrow.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Did you have any -- what did the people do to entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I suppose about the only thing I can recall is the, if you can call it entertainment, was probably played poker, rolled dice. Money -- you see, money was no object insofar as going to win. I don't know that all of us questioned whether or not we would ever come back, but from the standpoint of ever thinking we could win money, and there wasn't that much money available. So it was just a matter of a pastime, writing letters, playing different -- engaging in activities like poker and rolling of dice. That was about it.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Were there any entertainers that came to entertain you or your fellow shipmen?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No, ma'am. No, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Were you able to go on leave during any of the time?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No, not all the time that we were overseas, but a large percentage of our time was spent what we call four hours on and four hours off. All the time that we were near the enemy, also, and most of the time when we were at sea we were always cognizant of the fact that submarines possibility was around us and we were always on guard for that, even though we may not be on duty. But we were actually on duty four hours; off duty four hours. When you were on duty, you were generally above deck at a gunning station ready to participate in whatever activity may develop. And when you were off duty, you had the duty of cleaning. Aboard ship you were always aware of cleanliness. You constantly had to make sure that your surroundings as well as your physical body was clean, just in case you were injured. Plus the fact to keep down any disease, we were always cleaning the ship.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Do you recall any particularly humorous or unusual event?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No, I don't.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Were there ever any pranks that you played on each other or pulled any pranks on each other?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Not to my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: What did you think of your fellow sailors and your officers?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: For the most part, I would say for the large part, it was a very close-knit, compassionate acceptability of those around us, recognizing that they were enduring what you were enduring and that what was good for one was good for all.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Do you recall the day that your service ended?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Yes, very much so. I was -- my last service was off the coast of South America aboard a dry dock which we were repairing damaged ships. This was after I had come back from Europe. I didn't put that in there. I was in Trinidad for a considerable length of time. And I suppose from the standpoint of highs and lows, my low was about two o'clock in the morning on April the 12th when I learned by way of shortwave radio the death of President Roosevelt. That was almost as devastating as it would have been had I heard that my own father had died. That was certainly a tremendous blow. But then, of course, at a time was when I learned, sometime in March, I believe it was, that I was to be separated from service and would be coming home. I had never been -- I had never flown before and I was put aboard an old C-47, C-46 type plane that paratroopers jump from, somewhat like riding on a two-horse wagon over the rough terrain and rough seas and terrain in South America, coming home and landed in Miami. And then was transported by train up to Jacksonville, Florida, and then given a ticket to Columbus, Georgia, and I rode across South Georgia on a Greyhound bus and I was met at the Greyhound Bus Station, which is now, I believe, Country's Barbecue, in downtown Columbus by my mother and daddy.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: What did you do in the days and weeks after you got out of the Service?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I wanted to be a professional baseball player. We never had any baseball, what you might call organized in Cataula, although I made what they call, what they had, what they called was a men's baseball team back when I was 14 years old. It wasn't that I was all that good; we just didn't have that -- we just didn't have that many young fellows that could tolerate, was interested in playing in the hot sun on a Sunday afternoon playing baseball. But that's what I wanted to be. And I went and signed up, made the team. At that time they had a professional team being organized in Georgia and Alabama, and I played professional baseball for a few months with the LaGrange Troupers. I thought I was -- it would be equivalent today of paying a shortstop for the New York Yankees. I made a total of $150 a month. So you can imagine how wonderful that must have been for me.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Quite different than today.

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Did you go to work or did you go back to school?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I went to work. Of course, I went to a drug store and there was a young lady there that was a, kind of a waitress, cashier. And I thought that she -- she made eyes at me; I made eyes at her and the next thing I knew we were married. And I thought -- in a couple years we had a little boy and I drifted around from one type of job to another and recognized that I needed some education and I went off to college. And that was some four years later, actually. And the North Koreans invaded South Korea and I had joined the Army Reserve there at Shaw State and the Army decided they needed me and I was called back into the service during the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: What did you do during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I was a training sergeant. They promoted me from Boatswain's Mate to Master Sergeant and was made training sergeant of a battalion headquarters in the Chemical Corps and we ended up over at Fort McClellan and went to the Radiological, Biological, and Bacteriological Warfare School which at that time we were so tremendously concerned about the possibilities of atomic energy because that was a very short time -- when I say short time, it was about four years after we had dropped the atomic bomb -- and chemical and Communism went kind of hand in hand from the standpoint of national fear. And so I was in the Chemical Corps.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Was that in the Army or still the Navy at that time?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: That was in the Army. Yes, you see, when I was in school I was on the G.I. Bill which made it possible for Veterans to become educated if they wanted to be. And I wanted to be and I learned that on the college campus which was a small college down in Shaw, Alabama. It's a large university now. But they had an Army Reserve Unit and most of the young boys at that time or young men at that time were joining up trying to fulfill their military obligations because all young men had military obligations then. Although I had fulfilled mine by being in active service during World War II, at this time they needed ranking individuals, which I had in the Service, and they told me that they would give me the same rank in the Army that I had in the Navy. Well, when I was in school under the G.I. Bill and being married with a child, I was getting free tuition plus $120 a month. See I couldn't -- I didn't have time to work. So we were trying to get by on $120 a month, which was rather difficult, living down on the campus in an old trailer, they had a little trailer, they got some trailers from the war and some barracks from the old World War II, so this is four years after World War II. And so that I would -- if I would join the reserve, I would get $60 every three months and they would also give me the same rank, which was a Sergeant First Class. And so I wanted to know right quick where I sign because I wanted that $60 every three months. Well, I signed up, and lo and behold, I never got my first check before the North Koreans crossed the 38th parallel and created the Korean War and they called me back into active duty. So I -- and then I was called in with a chemical service company and this chemical service company, once we got activated and on a military base up at Fort McLellan, Alabama, they needed to form battalions which were the battalions are a higher or larger unit and the battalion generally has anywhere from three to five companies within it and they needed someone with military -- more experience so they elevated me into the battalion headquarters and made me a Master Sergeant.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Were you an instructor during that time?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Well, yes, ma'am, I was a trainer. I took and lectured, prepared lesson plans and so forth and taught people about the radiological and biological -- we were very concerned about the effects of chemical warfare, not only the alpha, beta, and gamma rays, which is the result of an atomic blast, but also all of the other chemicals that may be -- we may be subjected to at that time in Korea, because we were very, we were very fearful that the gas would be -- that gases would be used and that we had such things as mustard gas and different things and we were trying to not only show the men how to protect themselves but also how to -- how to combat against those kind of things.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: So after the Korean War did you go back to school and finish or what did you do after that?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No, ma'am. I had -- I had -- I did not have to go to Korea and I had had a strong desire cultivated sometime, I guess, while I was in high school because I always used to like to sketch and write and had little or no opportunity to do that in school because my graduating class of only 11 in my high school graduating class up in Hamilton in 1943. So I wanted to -- I wanted to gain more knowledge along that line. And while I was in the military up at Fort McClellan for two years, I signed up with a school out of Scranton, Pennsylvania, known as International Correspondence School and took an advertising and marketing course. But I didn't -- I didn't finish it for two years -- about two and a half years after I came out of the Service where I could -- it took me about five years to ever get my diploma. And quite pleasing to myself, I learned that when I received my diploma that only -- that less than 2 percent of the people who enrolled in correspondence classes, courses, ever finished. But I just had a strong determination to do that. And then when I came out of the Service in the Korean War, I went to work for the Columbus Ledger-Enquirer newspapers and worked for them for three and a half years. And I wanted all of that time to develop the skills to have myself an advertising marketing agency. And in 1956 I opened an advertising and marketing agency and I operated it for 28 years.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: While you were in the Service, did you develop any close friendships?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Yes, ma'am, but I was not able to -- not that I was not able to, I didn't exert the effort. I guess my best answer to that was I did have some very close relationships but -- but my current at-home obligations and I came from a large family. And any way that I could be of assistance to them, I guess I subconsciously, as well as to a degree consciously, I put my emphasis there and on my family and I neglected or was not financially capable of going and visiting those people. So therefore, those associations just fell by the wayside. And I regret it, but that's the way it happened.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Do you belong to any Veterans' organizations?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No, ma'am. I did, I believe, join with the American Legion for a while. I don't know, I guess -- two tours of duty and then a period of about seven or eight years in establishing a family and trying to establish a business of my own, by no means had any disregard for the Veterans' Associations, I just, I guess, placed my emphasis more on under my own roof.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Oh, definitely it did that. I don't suppose it could be otherwise. It's a puzzling thing always why people find it desirous to even think that anything is settled by wars. Just they are a necessity, yes, but there's -- they are -- it appears to be always some evil forces around, just as what we're confronted with today, and maybe one day--. But, yes, it did.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: How did your service and experience affect your life?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I suppose it gave me an appreciation for life and appreciation for our society. I'm always befuddled how our society seems to be so wrapped up either within themselves or with greed or other things that we don't really comprehend what we have here between the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, between the Canadian border and the Rio Grande River. I think that if we remember that the miracle of America almost approaches the miracle of Christ. We just -- we just don't do enough individual thinking, individual expression, and individuals exert individual efforts that can make this country so much greater than what it presently is.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: I understand that you wrote a book.

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: I wrote a pamphlet or a book, yes. I thought that back in 1985 that we were going somewhat in the wrong direction so far as opening our markets to too great of an extent of foreign products and foreign investors and I think it's come to pass. It was a little book, I think my title was we were giving America away, we were making it too easy. See, prior to World War II we were somewhat of an isolationist-type country. We may have closed our borders too much, but on the other hand, if we look now, don't we all pretty much agree that we have opened our borders far too much. I don't know where the balance was. I was not a politician, although I like to think that my knowledge of history is sufficient for me to make certain statements and certain claims. And at that time I was very fearful that we were going too much in the direction and I think that time has proven that to be right. But the whole thing is the horse is out of the barn now. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: Is there anything that you'd like to add to the interview that I may have not covered?

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: No, ma'am. I think perhaps I may have said too much. No, I don't -- I don't know -- I mean I just -- I just wish that we all -- when I say "all," I'm pointing back to myself, that we really understood more thoroughly and that especially our young people and that our young couples, our young people marrying and divorcing in just in the matter of a very short time and then, you know, I'm no authority there, but the reason but I just -- I just think that our stick-to-it-iveness, our dedication, our sincere effort -- I don't mean necessarily walking down the street every day and lecturing others, but I'm just -- I'm heartbroken that we don't appreciate more of what we have. I think that's about the extent of my remarks.

sp.speaker: Rebecca Blair
sp.p: I want to thank you so much for your service to your country and I want to thank you for doing the interview with us and for sharing with us.

sp.speaker: Charles Douglas Pritchett
sp.p: Thank you, ma'am. I wish you well. (End of interview.)
